To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the new biology of the heart and lungs has great potential for advancing our understanding of the pathogenesis of congenital heart disease, bronchopulmonary disorders, and other cardiopulmonary disorders, that research on these disorders requires sophisticated infrastructures and cores, and that training and support for clinician-scientist is essential to translate basic research to clinical outcomes.

1. the new biology of the cardiopulmonary systems has the potential to transform the way we understand and treat cardiopulmonary disease; 2. the new biology will require collaborative, multidisciplinary research supported by core facilities and infrastructures; 3. the new biology has the capacity to transform the way in which we train and support the next generation of clinician-sciences; and 4. the research initiatives will require networks for translational research and clinical implementation.

(1) there are many opportunities in the new biology to study cardiopulmonary development and disease, but (2) there are many barriers that prevent the development and support of clinican-scientists who can translate the new biology into clinical outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying the development of the heart and lungs, the mechanisms underlying congenital heart disease, and the mechanisms underlying bronchopulmonary disease.
the development, maturation, and function of the cardiopulmonary systems, and the translation of basic research findings to the clinical setting.
the development of novel approaches and strategies to prevent or treat cardiopulmonary disease in the fetus, newborn, and adult.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cardiopulmonary research and training opportunities are limited and need to be expanded.
the new biology is a rich source of new insights, but the training of clinician-scholars is essential for the translation of basic science to clinical outcomes.
the new biology of the cardiopulmonary systems provides the basis for a new era of discovery and innovation in cardiology and pediatric pulmonology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to train more clinician-scientist, and that we need to support the training and research of those who are already here.
we need to train the clinician-scientist workforce and provide the infrastructure and support to enable the clinician-sciences to conduct research that will improve the care of our patients.
the new biology is poised to provide mechanistic insight into cardiopulmonary development and disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the new biology has the power to provide mechanistic insight into complex cardiopulmonic diseases.
the training of clinician-scholars in cardiology and in neonatology is essential to the future of pediatric cardiovascular and respiratory medicine.
